oneSentence: Use of AI tools outside approved organisational processes, especially where data, security, legal or oversight rules are bypassed.
plainExplanation:
This term means staff use an AI tool that their organisation has not approved, reviewed or connected to its normal rules. The tool might be public, privately bought, or added by a team without central oversight. The input can be a prompt, a document, meeting notes, code or spreadsheet data. The output can be a summary, draft, translation, analysis or recommendation.

What happens in the middle is the main risk. Because the tool sits outside approved processes, the organisation may not know what data was entered, where that data was stored, who can access it, or how the tool uses it. It may also be unclear whether the tool keeps prompts, uses them for further training, shares them with other services, or applies proper access control, meaning rules about who can see or do what.

The result may look useful, so the practice can spread quickly. But the organisation loses visibility and control. Security teams may be unable to monitor use. Legal and policy teams may not be able to check contracts, retention rules or human rights implications. Leaders may think AI use is limited when, in practice, it is already affecting real work.

Shadow AI is related to shadow IT, which means unapproved technology use more broadly. It is not the same as an AI attack such as prompt injection or data poisoning, though it can make those problems more likely because safeguards are missing. It is also not the same as confidentiality itself: confidentiality is the requirement to protect information, while shadow AI is one way that requirement can be put at risk.

everydayAnalogy.title: A private translation app used for office notes
everydayAnalogy.story: A team in Nairobi and Bogotá needs quick translations during a busy week. One colleague starts using a free phone app to translate draft meeting notes because the approved service feels slow. Soon others send the app short extracts, names and schedule details because the translations come back in seconds. The work gets done faster, but no one in the organisation knows what was uploaded, whether the app stores it, or who can view it later.

mapping.analogyElement: Free phone translation app used without approval

mapping.aiElement: Organisational data entered into the tool

mapping.analogyElement: Fast translations encourage more people to use it
No one knows what the app keeps or shares
mapping.aiElement: Loss of oversight over storage, access and data handling

everydayAnalogy.limitation: This analogy focuses on data leaving the organisation, but shadow AI is broader. It can also involve locally installed tools, browser plug-ins or team-built systems that never send data to a public app but still bypass approval, logging, procurement or security review. Also, not every unapproved use involves sensitive data; the core issue is lack of authorised oversight, not only secrecy.

visual.title: How shadow AI appears and why it becomes a risk
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, the reader should be able to explain how a useful shortcut turns into a governance and security problem.
visual.description: A left-to-right sequence of four labelled boxes. Read from first use to organisational impact. Each box shows one stage: work pressure, unapproved tool use, hidden data flow, and loss of oversight. Arrows show how convenience leads to repeated use and then to unmanaged risk.

steps.label: Work need
steps.explanation: A person has a task such as summarising notes, translating text or drafting a reply under time pressure.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a document icon and a clock inside a rounded box labelled 'Work need'.

steps.label: Quick shortcut
steps.explanation: The person uses an AI tool that has not been approved or reviewed because it is easy to access.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a laptop and a sparkle icon in a second box labelled 'Unapproved tool' with an arrow from step 1.

steps.label: Hidden data flow
steps.explanation: Text, files or metadata move into the tool, but the organisation may not know what was entered, stored or shared.
steps.visualInstruction: Show arrows from a document into a cloud-shaped box, with a small question mark badge, labelled 'Unknown handling'.

steps.label: Loss of oversight
steps.explanation: Security, legal and managers cannot apply normal checks such as access control, retention rules, monitoring or procurement review.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a shield, checklist and eye icon faded or crossed in a fourth box labelled 'Controls bypassed'.

visual.interaction: On hover or tap, each step expands to show one example: summarising notes, translating text, uploading a spreadsheet, or using a browser plug-in.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram presents four stages in order. First, a worker has a time-pressured task such as summarising or translating. Second, they choose an AI tool that the organisation has not approved because it is fast and easy. Third, work content or data goes into that tool, but the organisation may not know what data was entered, where it is stored, or who can access it. Fourth, because the tool sits outside approved processes, normal controls such as access restrictions, monitoring, retention rules and legal review are bypassed. The overall message is that convenience can lead to hidden AI use and then to unmanaged risk.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-box sequence with arrows, showing the same stages without animation: work need, unapproved tool, hidden data flow, and controls bypassed.

workedExample.scenario: A small policy team has 120 open-ended survey comments in English, Arabic and French and wants a quick thematic summary before a meeting.
workedExample.input: A staff member copies 30 comments at a time into a public AI chatbot from a personal browser account and asks for themes and a draft briefing note.
process: The staff member chooses the public tool because it is immediately available and not blocked.
They paste survey text, including village names and a few respondent details, into the chatbot.
The tool returns a clear-looking summary with four themes and suggested wording for the briefing note.
The team uses the draft, but the organisation has no record of what text was uploaded, what account was used, or what terms governed data retention.
workedExample.result: The team saves time, but the organisation now faces an unmanaged risk: potentially sensitive information was processed outside approved oversight, and leaders may not even know the tool is part of the workflow.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN office wants to analyse household assessment survey responses to identify common service needs across districts. An employee considers using a public AI assistant to cluster open-text answers and draft a summary.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: This is a realistic case because AI can seem helpful for large volumes of text, especially when teams are under deadline pressure. If the tool is unapproved, the office may lose control over data handling, retention, accountability and quality review.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not paste personal data, household-level responses, location details, protection-sensitive information or any confidential assessment content into an unapproved public AI service. Use only approved tools and keep human oversight over analysis and reporting.

whyItMatters: For non-specialists, this matters because it changes risk without looking like a security incident. A team may simply be trying to save time, yet the organisation can lose sight of what data is being processed, which vendors are involved, what contractual terms apply, and whether outputs are being checked. That affects confidentiality, records management, procurement, legal compliance, auditability and trust. For leaders, shadow AI can create a false picture: the organisation may appear cautious on paper while unapproved tools are already shaping drafts, analysis and decisions in practice. Good decisions require visibility, approved pathways and clear rules for when AI may or may not be used.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Shadow AI only means staff are secretly misbehaving.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Not necessarily. It often starts with ordinary work pressure and a useful shortcut. People may not realise a tool is unapproved, may assume free consumer services are harmless, or may not know the organisation has separate rules for public and approved systems.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If no obvious hack happened, there is no security issue.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Security is not only about someone breaking in. Risk also comes from data going into systems outside approved controls, from unclear storage and retention, from weak access rules, and from outputs being used without review. The harm can come from process gaps, not dramatic intrusion.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Shadow AI is the same as data exfiltration.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They overlap but are not identical. Data exfiltration means data is taken out without authorisation. Shadow AI is broader: it includes any unapproved AI use, even if no sensitive data was entered. A harmless-seeming draft request can still be shadow AI because oversight was bypassed.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: People use an AI tool for work without the organisation approving or supervising it.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Shadow AI is the use of AI systems, models, plug-ins or AI-enabled services outside established organisational governance. Typical gaps include missing procurement review, absent security assessment, unclear data-processing terms, unmanaged identities and access, no logging or monitoring, and no defined retention or deletion controls. Inputs may include prompts, files, metadata or connected service data. Outputs may then enter formal workflows despite the tool sitting outside approved architecture and policy. The security issue is therefore not only model behaviour; it is the loss of visibility and enforceable controls around data handling, access, audit and accountability. The term is related to shadow IT, but focuses on AI-specific uses and integrations.

keyTakeaway: The main danger is not that the tool looks advanced; it is that work and data can move outside approved oversight without anyone noticing.

quickCheck.question: Which example best fits shadow AI?
options: A staff member uses an organisation-approved AI tool under the published rules.
A team pastes work material into a public AI service because it is faster, even though the service has not been approved.
A model gives an inaccurate summary and the team corrects it before use.
An attacker tricks a chatbot with a hidden instruction in a web page.
quickCheck.explanation: Shadow AI is about unapproved AI use outside normal governance. Option 2 fits because the tool is being used for work without approval or oversight. Option 4 describes indirect prompt injection, which is an attack type, not the governance problem itself.

contested: The exact boundary varies by organisation. Some use the term only for public generative AI tools, while others include any AI capability adopted without formal approval, including local models, browser extensions and vendor features quietly added to existing software.

issues.problem: The definition of data exfiltration is too broad and contradicts the supplied distinct entry. Unauthorised movement alone is not the full definition. The information must be copied to a place an attacker or unapproved user can access.
issues.fix: They can overlap but are not identical. Data exfiltration is unauthorised copying to a place an attacker or unapproved user can access. Shadow AI is unapproved AI use, even if no information reaches such a place. A harmless-seeming draft request can still be shadow AI because oversight was bypassed.

issues.problem: The statement that security, legal and managers "cannot apply" normal checks is absolute and false. Unapproved use can bypass procurement or prior review while still being visible to network monitoring or subject to some existing controls.
issues.fix: Normal checks such as procurement review, logging, access control or retention rules may be missing or harder to enforce.

issues.problem: The accessibility text repeats the false absolute claim that normal controls are bypassed. Shadow AI creates gaps in oversight, but it does not guarantee that every listed control is absent or ineffective.
issues.fix: Fourth, because the tool sits outside approved processes, normal checks such as access restrictions, monitoring, retention rules and legal review may be missing or harder to enforce.

issues.problem: The marked answer is uniquely best, but the explanation considers only options 2 and 4. It does not explain that option 1 is approved or that option 3 establishes an accuracy problem rather than unapproved use. Options 3 and 4 could coexist with shadow AI, but neither states the defining condition.
issues.fix: Option 2 states unapproved AI use. Option 1 is approved. Option 3 shows an accuracy issue. Option 4 shows indirect prompt injection. The last two could coexist with shadow AI, but neither example establishes it.
